question: What is the main goal of a retrospective research study?

options.A: Testing a new drug in real time

explanation: Great job! Think of 'retrospective' like looking in a rearview mirror—these studies look backward at data or events that already happened instead of following people forward. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why would a nurse researcher choose a retrospective study to look into a very rare disease?

options.A: It costs nothing to access and analyze hospital databases
options.B: It proves the exact cause of the disease without any doubt
options.C: Past records already contain enough accumulated cases to study
options.D: Patients prefer answering questions about their past illnesses

explanation: Spot on! Because rare conditions take forever to pop up in real-time studies, looking backward at existing hospital records lets researchers gather enough cases right away. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h1)

question: Which study type compares patients who have a specific illness with those who don't, checking to see what they were exposed to in the past?
explanation: You've got this! A case-control study starts with the final outcome (like having the disease) and looks backward to compare who was exposed to a risk factor and who wasn't. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h2)

question: A nurse wants to check old hospital files of patients who took a specific blood pressure drug five years ago to see who developed kidney issues. What kind of study is this?
explanation: Well done! This design starts with a past exposure (the drug taken years ago) and tracks forward through old records to see what health outcomes happened. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h2)

question: What is a major source of information when conducting a retrospective nursing study?
explanation: Correct! Since retrospective research relies on things that already happened, electronic health records (EHRs) are a goldmine for this kind of data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h3)

question: Why is using a standard checklist or form important when reviewing old patient charts?

options.A: It automatically prevents all forms of patient bias
options.B: It ensures every chart is checked for the same consistent variables
options.C: It allows the researcher to change the research question midway
options.D: It replaces the need for ethical approval from the hospital

explanation: Exactly! Using a standard form keeps your data collection neat, uniform, and organized, even when you're looking through hundreds of different patient folders. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h3)

question: What is one of the biggest perks of doing retrospective research instead of starting a brand new study?

options.A: It completely eliminates all measurement errors
options.B: It does not require any ethical review
options.C: It proves direct cause and effect every time
options.D: It is faster and less expensive to conduct

explanation: Spot on! Because the patients have already been treated and the data is already sitting there, you save a ton of time and money compared to starting from scratch. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h4)

question: Why must a researcher use a retrospective study rather than a live experiment when studying the health effects of a toxic chemical spill?

options.A: It is unethical to intentionally expose people to toxins
options.B: People exposed to toxins refuse to talk to researchers
options.C: Historical records are always one hundred percent accurate
options.D: Prospective studies cannot measure chemical levels accurately

explanation: You nailed it! We can never put people in harm's way on purpose. Looking backward at an accidental past exposure is the only safe, ethical way to study it. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h4)

question: What does 'recall bias' mean in a retrospective study?

options.A: The loss of physical paper charts in a fire
options.B: Difficulty or inaccuracy in remembering past events
options.C: A computer error when deleting electronic patient files
options.D: The refusal of a hospital to share old records

explanation: Correct! Recall bias happens when patients struggle to accurately remember or report details about things that happened to them a long time ago. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a limitation or downside of retrospective research?

options.A: Proving definitive cause and effect relationships easily
options.B: Being vulnerable to inaccurate historical documentation
options.C: Dealing with missing information in old medical charts
options.D: Struggling with inconsistent nursing notes from the past

explanation: Well spotted! Retrospective studies actually struggle to prove cause and effect, so proving it easily is definitely NOT a feature of this design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h5)

question: Do retrospective studies that only use old patient charts still need ethical approval?

options.A: No, because the patients have already been discharged
options.B: Only if the study is funded by a pharmaceutical company
options.C: Yes, approval from an ethics committee or IRB is still required
options.D: Only if more than one thousand charts are reviewed

explanation: Spot on! Even though the patients aren't actively in the hospital anymore, their health information is still private and protected, so ethical clearance is a must. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h6)

question: Why is removing patient names and personal details (de-identifying) so important in chart review studies?

options.A: To protect patient privacy and confidentiality
options.B: To satisfy financial auditors from the hospital
options.C: To prevent missing data from appearing in the results
options.D: To make the data collection process go much faster

explanation: You got it! Patient confidentiality is sacred in nursing. Stripping away names ensures nobody's private medical history is exposed during your research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h6)
